1:
The chapter carries no date, and none can be fixed. John Gill rules out the famine at the siege of Jerusalem, since that affected only the city while this affected all Judea, and reports two guesses: early in the reign of Zedekiah, or in that of Jehoiakim, when a fast is recorded which may have been on this occasion. Charles Ellicott agrees that no such calamity is mentioned in the account of the prophet’s life, but reasons from a later verse implying he had already suffered scorn that the period is not earlier than Jehoiakim. Adam Clarke supposes the discourse delivered after the fourth year of that reign, but doubts whether any particular dearth is meant, this being a standing risk of the climate: scarcely any rain fell from April to mid-October, and the winter rain was kept in tanks, so a dry winter made a dearth unavoidable. John Calvin takes the passage as prophecy, not record, and explains why it had to come before the event. Whenever adversity comes the causes are sought in the world, so that hardly anyone regards the hand that smites; in a year of sterility we consult astrology and think it owing to the stars, and God’s judgment is passed over. The drought had therefore to be pointed out before it was manifest, that the Jews might know it did not happen by chance.

Matthew Henry reads the opening verse as the title of the chapter, and answers an objection. Much of what follows is prayer rather than oracle, yet these are not unfitly called the word of the Lord which came to him, for every acceptable prayer is one God puts into our hearts, and nothing is our word that comes to him but what is first his word that comes from him. Keil and Delitzsch set the passage in its frame: the drought gives occasion for urgent prayer, the Lord rejects all intercession and gives notice of destruction by sword, famine and pestilence, and the discourse is not a single address but a summary of utterances concerning the calamity. Clarke adds a comment on its shape: though forbidden to intercede, the prophet falls on the happy expedient of introducing the people as supplicating in their own name the mercy he was not allowed to ask in his.

The description that follows is admired for its manner. Calvin explains why so many figures are used where one sentence would serve: he might have said simply that there would be a grievous famine, but hardly one in a hundred would be moved by words so plainly expressed, and to arouse their stupor he uses the most forcible terms. The past tense is used of what is future, to show its certainty. On the gates, Clarke and Ellicott agree that the word stands figuratively for the inhabitants, the gates being places of public concourse; Ellicott compares them to the market-place of a Greek city and pictures the people in black garments of sorrow crouching on the ground. Henry notes what the mourning is not for: Judah mourns for the trouble and not the sin, for the withholding of the rain and not the withdrawing of God’s favour; the gates through which corn used to come now look melancholy, the inhabitants departing through them to seek bread abroad. On the little ones sent for water, Gill and Ellicott take them for menial servants, the word being peculiar to this prophet; Clarke reads it the other way, that servants no longer attended their lords and the nobles had to employ their own children. Calvin makes the point authority, not kinship: they sent them by command, as the great constrain the common sort. Ellicott adds that covering the head is the extremest sign of a grief too great to utter, and recalls its use in an ancient painting of a father at a daughter’s sacrifice.
4:
The picture widens from the city to the land, and the first word is disputed. Charles Ellicott admits that the rendering chapt describes so vividly the fissures a drought opens in the soil that one gives it up with reluctance, but no such meaning is found in the Hebrew word, which simply means is struck with terror; the translators apparently followed an older version giving languishes for thirst, and so, applied to the earth, cracked. He observes that as the gates earlier stood for the people of the city, the ground stands here in visible sympathy with the tillers of the soil, and finds an almost awful pathos in the repeated covering of heads, city and country alike plunged into the utter blackness of despair. John Gill gives both senses, that the ground is chapt through violent heat and want of rain, or is broken and crumbles into dust. John Calvin presses the second: when the heavens supply moisture the earth keeps its solid character, but in a great heat we see it dissolving into dust as though pounded in a mortar. The shame that follows is more than sorrow—it makes the husbandmen shun the light and the sight of men; and all of it was to make the Jews know that they were not deprived of water by chance, but because God had cursed their land so that it yielded no water even for the common wants of nature.

The two animals named are chosen for what is unnatural in their behaviour. Ellicott corrects the connective, the verse giving the reason for the terror rather than adding to it, and notes that each region has its representative instance of misery: the hind, noted for its tenderness to its young, abandons it to seek pasture for itself and finds none. Calvin makes the same point at length. Hinds wander in solitary places and seek their food there, having a natural timidity which keeps them from exposing themselves; but here famine constrains them to come out to the plains, bring forth there and flee away, though they prefer their young to their own life. They come down because there is no grass in the mountains and the woods. John Wesley puts the same reversal plainly, that these loving creatures could not suckle their young once their moisture was dried up, and were forced to leave them and run about seeking grass. Gill supplies natural history instead, that hinds sometimes cast their young through fear, common in heat and drought, and that a naturalist reports the harts of Syria breeding on the highest mountains on the borders of the land.

The wild asses are read the same way. Ellicott turns from the field to the bare hill-tops and finds a scene of like distress, the wild asses seeming turned into beasts of prey and standing gaping for thirst as jackals pant for their prey; he corrects the received dragons to jackals, notes that some scholars take the word for crocodiles with their wide gaping jaws, and observes that the herbage named here is ranker than that on which the hind fed. Adam Clarke proposes the hippopotamus, which after feeding under water must come to the surface to take in fresh draughts of air, or else the wild asses themselves. Wesley reports the older explanation, that dragons ordinarily stand on high places sucking in the cool air, citing two ancient naturalists for it. Calvin reasons from the animal’s endurance: the wild ass can bear want for a long time, so that its failure is itself a remarkable evidence of vengeance; burning with long famine, they seek food in the wind itself. Gill offers a different reading of the high places, that one version renders the word brooks, so that the asses came as usual to drink, found the streams dried up, and stood distressed and not knowing where to go.
7:
The prayer that follows is in the first person plural, and John Calvin asks why the prophet includes himself. He does not assume the character of others as if free from guilt, since he was not more righteous than Daniel, who confessed not only the people’s sins but his own; though not one of God’s despisers he was one of the people, and connects himself with them sincerely. He also asks why the prayer was published rather than offered silently at home, and answers that it was to rouse the people by his example. This shows the design of the prediction: the scarcity was announced so that they might through repentance escape the wrath of God, who even with the sword drawn may still be pacified. John Gill identifies the speaker the same way, as the prophet interceding and confessing their sins and his own. Charles Ellicott notes the turn from the picture of suffering to the prayer, and the conviction beneath it, that the drought has not come without cause and calls men to repentance. On the petition he prefers a more general rendering—not do thou it but act thou—not according to the rigour of justice but according to the Name which witnesses of mercy and long-suffering. John Wesley and Adam Clarke read it as a request for rain sought on no ground but that name, since they deserve nothing but death.

The titles given to God next are what the plea rests on. Calvin explains the confidence: it is on the ground of the covenant that he prays God to glorify his name, and such a prayer could not be made for heathen nations. He is careful about the word hope. It is not that the Israelites relied on God as they ought, for the ten tribes had long since revolted and such corruption prevailed in Judah that hardly one in a thousand could be called faithful; hope among them had become extinct. The word refers instead to God’s promise and the constancy of his faithfulness: unworthy as we are of protection, yet as thou hast promised to be always ready to help, thou art our hope. The second title he refers to past proofs of that help in distress. Gill takes the first as naming the author, object and foundation of hope for all good things.

The two similes that follow are daring, and handled carefully. Ellicott says no image could paint more vividly the sense of abandonment weighing on the prophet: Israel had looked to God as its watchful guardian, and now he seemed as indifferent as a passing traveller is to the interests of the city in whose inn he lodges for a night. Clarke turns the figure into petition: instead of dwelling among us thou hast scarcely paid the most transient visit to thy land; come once more and dwell among us. Keil and Delitzsch take the second pair as an appeal to God’s power, since he cannot let himself look like a man at his wit’s end or a nerveless warrior, which is how he would seem if he did not help. On the rare word they follow a derivation from the Arabic giving one who by sudden mischance has lost his presence of mind, which suits the comparison with a warrior who has no strength to help. Calvin reports the same crop of renderings—sleeping, wandering, weak, astonished, surprised—and one further, that it means a person who rushes to help someone in danger and cannot deliver him. He reads the second figure as a strong helper of no skill, useless from his own bulk, and says the strange thing would be that God should be anxious to help and yet do nothing. Ellicott hears faith reviving in the last clause: God is more than the passing guest and abides among his people, and the closing words mean they are still recognised as his.
10:
The answer, when it comes, goes past the prophet to the people. John Gill notes that instead of answering directly God speaks to them and makes their sin the cause of his conduct, calling them not his people but this people, they having broken covenant with him. Matthew Henry reads the exchange as the dispute between the owner and the dresser of the vineyard over the barren fig-tree, the owner’s justice condemning it and the dresser’s clemency interceding for a reprieve. God tells the prophet they are not duly qualified for pardon. There was hope if they returned; but this people show no disposition to return, and their backslidings have been their choice and pleasure, which should have been their shame. Sinners are wanderers from God; the aggravation here is that they love to wander, and cannot expect God to rest with them while they delight in going astray after their idols. John Calvin takes the wandering as inconstancy, set against the quietness another prophet prescribed. They would not rely on God’s help, but ran here and there for vain helps and after idols; their confederacies with the Egyptians and the Chaldeans cost them much, when they might have waited quietly for the aid promised them. He observes that the opening particle is given in none of the versions, and suggests it answers the previous complaint: God had been called a traveller who makes no stay, and the reply is that they themselves loved to wander. Charles Ellicott makes the connection differently, taking the opening word to point back to the backslidings confessed in the prayer; the second half of the verse quotes Hosea verbatim, and the emphasis falls on now being the time for remembering iniquity.

The prohibition of prayer is the hardest thing here, and it is handled three ways. Adam Clarke states its severity without softening: they are ripe for destruction, and how dreadful is the state of a people about whom the Lord says to his ministers, pray not for them—or withholds from them the spirit of intercession. Ellicott finds in it the sternest part of the prophet’s work, to feel that even the prayer that punishment may be averted is unaccepted. Calvin limits it. The prohibition is to be understood of the exile only, since God had decreed the banishment and that decree was immutable; it is not a general ban on asking forgiveness for the people or for the godly who remained. He might still pray that God, satisfied with their temporal punishment, would spare the miserable as to eternal life, and might pray for the remnant. Unless this is borne in mind the prohibition seems strange, since it is among the first duties of love to be solicitous for one another before God. Keil and Delitzsch mark the passage as the Lord’s answer and set out its terms; John Wesley summarises the reply, that for their manifold sins he was resolved to punish them.

The rejection of fast and sacrifice raises the question whether the worship was insincere. Gill and Calvin say it was. Gill supposes a fast proclaimed on account of the dearth, at which they cried aloud and made a great noise, but their prayers being hypocritical were not accepted. Calvin says the words are addressed especially to hypocrites, since the declaration that God is near to all who call on him in sincerity remains unchangeable; the people wearied themselves pacifying God by an external profession and did nothing but act falsely. Ellicott declines to press it. We need not assume the fast and the sacrifice were hypocritical, though much of that doubtless mingled with the worship of Israel then as before; the lesson is rather that they came too late to stay the discipline of chastisement. On the three judgments he observes how constantly the latter plagues follow the former, so that the union of the three has become proverbial.
13:
The prophet answers the prohibition with an excuse for the people, and the commentators weigh whether it is a good one. John Gill explains the motive: he was grieved at heart because he was forbidden to pray and because the Lord had resolved on their ruin, and pitied them the more because they had been deceived by the false prophets, so that he tries to excuse them and lay the blame elsewhere. Adam Clarke states the plea and its rejection together—true, they are exceedingly wicked, but the false prophets have deceived them, which is some mitigation—and answers his own question as to why God does not admit it: the people believed those prophets without having any proof of their divine mission. John Calvin asks again why a private prayer is published, and answers as before, that it was not for boasting but for the people’s good; the colloquy with God availed much to touch the Jews, since as though present they were shown what he had heard from God’s mouth. He weighs the opening exclamation and allows two senses, grief and astonishment, preferring grief, though astonishment is not unsuitable, so that the Jews might feel horrified with him on seeing how they had been led astray. He notes that the word prophets is emphatic in the sentence.

Charles Ellicott gives the fullest account of what the prophet was up against. The colleges or schools of the prophets had degenerated from their first ideal and become corrupt and ambitious seekers after popularity, as the mendicant orders did later in Christendom; an earlier prophet whose words were still fresh had spoken sharply of the growing evil, and a later one devotes a whole chapter to prophets who followed their own spirit and had seen no true vision. Here the true prophet feels more bitterly than ever the misery of having to contend against that body. Ellicott sets the two messages side by side: to this prophet the future was clear, since the sins of the people must lead to shame, defeat and exile, and only through that discipline might they return to better days; the false prophets took the easier and more popular line of predicting victory and assured peace—literally, peace of truth.

The reply distinguishes the true message from the false and then examines how falsehood works. Ellicott enumerates the four forms named in the verse: the false vision, false as being only the dream of a disordered fancy; divination by signs and auguries, such as by arrows or by cups; a thing of nought, more accurately the small image of a god used as the household idols were, as in some way forecasting the future; and the deceit of their own heart, an imposture pure and simple, the fraud of a deliberately counterfeit inspiration. Clarke puts the same distinction more briefly, that they say they have visions but have them by divination and they are false; the people should know their character and avoid them, but they love to have it so and will not be undeceived. Calvin draws the general rule he thinks the passage exists to teach. We ought to beware of every appearance of falsehood and not believe all prophecies rashly or without discrimination, since not everything boasted of as divine is really so; God would have us wisely distinguish, and for that reason Calvin holds the passage to deserve special notice. He then applies the rule against the ecclesiastical claims of his own day, arguing that a body which asserts itself to be the true church and the pillar of truth cannot on that title alone confound the simple into accepting whatever it determines. Gill notes only that the answer replies to the excuse offered in the people’s favour, and Calvin observes that it is the more forcible for following the question, penetrating the mind more easily than a bare statement would.
15:
The sentence on the false prophets is the exact reverse of what they promised. Charles Ellicott states the principle: to the mind of a true prophet, feeling that he was taught of God, nothing could be more hateful than the acts of those who for selfish ends were leading the people to destruction, and for them there was therefore the righteous retribution that they should perish in the very calamities they had asserted would never come. Adam Clarke fills in the history behind it. The prophet had told the king that if he rebelled against Nebuchadnezzar he would be overthrown and the land wasted by sword and famine; the false prophets said there would be neither sword nor famine but peace and prosperity; the king believed them and withheld the tribute; the invasion followed and destroyed the land, and the false prophets fell in these calamities. John Gill notes only that the description that follows shows which prophets are meant.

The harder question is why the people who were deceived should share the punishment, and John Calvin devotes the passage to it. God might seem to deal hardly with them in inflicting so severe a punishment on men who had been misled, but the answer is evident: unless the world willingly sought falsehoods, the power of the devil to deceive would not be so great. When men are led astray by impostures it happens through their own fault, since they are readier to embrace vanity than to submit to God and his word; the reprobate are given up to a reprobate mind because they wilfully seek falsehood and will not obey the truth. On this account, he says, God declares that he tries the hearts of men whenever false prophets come abroad, for anyone who really fears God will not be led away by the deceits of impostors; and whenever men are too credulous and readily embrace deceptions, it is certain that their hypocrisy is being justly punished. He observes that the Jews had always wished for prophets who soothed their ears and promised an abundant harvest and a fruitful vintage; as they had itching ears, a liberty was justly given to falsehood to deluge the whole land, and so it happened.

Calvin closes the argument by shutting the door on complaint. The reason God so severely visited a people who had been deceived was their previous impiety and ingratitude, and the last word of the verse names it: a dreadful calamity awaits them, but that they may not complain of his severity, they receive the reward of their own wickedness. He allows that the word might mean punishment rather than wickedness, since a kindred term carries both senses, but prefers wickedness as giving the reason why God resolved on so dreadful a judgment. What the passage shows, he concludes, is that God does not heedlessly execute vengeance on the innocent, but that the teachers and the whole people who approved of them were involved in one punishment. He also proposes a different joining of the two verses, carrying the phrase these prophets over from the end of the first into the subject of the second, so that prophets and people together are cast out into the streets of Jerusalem; this construction he thinks evidently the best. Clarke states the same conclusion without the argument, that the people shall be destroyed because they preferred lying words to the truth proclaimed to them, and Gill limits the sentence to those of them who gave credit to the false prophecies.
17:
The prophet is now told to weep aloud, and the instruction is read as having a purpose. John Calvin explains it as a last resort against stupor. The people were so tardy that no threatening could bring them to a right mind, so God bids a sad spectacle be set before them; the prophet wept sincerely, but is told to declare this weeping to the whole people, not in secret. Since their obstinacy was such that they shed no tears though often terrified with dreadful threatenings, the coming calamity had to be set before their eyes in the person of the prophet. John Gill marks the substitution: instead of praying for the people he has a doleful lamentation put into his mouth, to assure them of what was coming and affect them with it. Matthew Henry hopes it means more. He takes the formula introducing it to cover the intercession that follows as well as the lament, so that it amounts to a revocation of the earlier direction not to pray; and in any case the prayers in these verses make it plain that the prophet took the earlier words not as a prohibition but as a discouragement. He pictures him standing over the ruins of his country, signifying that he foresaw the sword and another famine more grievous than the present—this in the country for want of rain, that in the city through the straitness of the siege. Charles Ellicott observes that though not in form a prediction, no words could express more emphatically the terrible nature of the judgments implied; the language is all but identical with what recurs in the Lamentations, and may be looked on as the germ of which those elegies were the development. Adam Clarke supplies the historical breach: the land was distressed first by one invading king, then laid under tribute by another, and afterwards nearly desolated by famine—three calamities within a few years, well called a great breach.

The eighteenth verse is admired for the completeness of the trap it describes. Calvin says the prophet repeats himself not because he was obscure but because he knew he spoke to the deaf and that their sloth needed many goads; the sum is that there would be no defence in the city and no safety in the fields. He speaks as though he saw it: the enemy destroys with drawn sword all who venture out, and famine kills those the enemy has not reached. Calvin prefers to read the two key words as nouns—the piercings of the sword, the wastings of the famine—and concludes that there would be no place of rest, since if they fled they met swords and if they hid they met famine, perishing without being destroyed by any enemy. Clarke describes a succession of frightful spectacles, the wounded, the dying, the starving and the slain, with none to bury the dead or bring relief. Ellicott presses the second clause for a stronger sense, that the word sums all individual sufferings in one collective unity—the sickness of famine, the pestilence that follows on starvation.

The last clause of the verse is disputed. Ellicott renders it literally as going about in a land and not knowing, and offers two possibilities: that prophet and priest are in exile and do not know where to find a home or where they may be dragged next, or that they learn no wisdom from their bitter experience; the marginal rendering he thinks has no adequate ground. Clarke takes them as obliged to leave the cities and wander in unfrequented places seeking the necessaries of life, and reports another scholar’s suggestion that they went trafficking about with their false doctrines as pedlars do with their wares, seeking their own gain—a reading he declines. Gill locates the going forth simply, as outside the city where the besieging camp lay.
19:
The prophet returns to intercession in spite of the ban, and the commentators note that he does. Charles Ellicott puts it most directly: the heart of the patriot overpowers the conviction of the prophet, and though bidden not to pray he bursts forth with a prayer of passionate intercession. John Calvin gives the act a further purpose. The prophet turns to prayer that by his example he might rouse the people to lamentation, so that they might humbly implore forgiveness; and he indirectly reproves their hardness, for having effected nothing by teaching he changed his manner of speaking, and leaving the people addressed God. John Gill observes simply that though forbidden he proceeds to prayers and expostulations on account of these people.

The two verbs of the question are pressed for their force. Calvin distinguishes them, the first meaning to reject with contempt, the second to reject with abhorrence—had he despised Judah as a worthless thing and abhorred Zion as a filthy one? Ellicott says the Hebrew of the second implies the act of rejection as well as the feeling that leads to it. Both find the argument of the prayer in what has been promised. Calvin says the prophet reasons from what is inconsistent: God had promised he should ever have a lamp at Jerusalem; the ten tribes had been wholly demolished, yet a seed remained because Judah continued, the flower of the whole people, from which the salvation of the world was to proceed. The expostulation runs, thou hast chosen this tribe that it might be safe perpetually, commanded the temple to be built on that mount for thy name, and said it would be thy rest for ever. Gill makes the same appeal a series of exclamations—Judah, whom the Lord had chosen and where his dwelling place was; Judah, from whom the chief ruler was to come; Judah, from whom the sceptre was not to depart—and asks whether this tribe, on which so many favours were bestowed, could be utterly rejected. Adam Clarke reads the disappointed expectation historically, that they looked for prosperity when the king purged the land of idolatry, and found no good because they relapsed into their former ways.

The confession that follows is treated as the model of what such a prayer should be. Calvin says the prophet is prescribing the way of appeasing God, and explains why he speaks in the plural when hardly one in a thousand knew their sin: he does not assume the character of the whole people, but dictates for posterity a right form of prayer, so that in exile they might know that this one thing remained—to confess their sins, since otherwise they could not obtain pardon. He is careful that confession here stands for repentance and not for the freedom with which hypocrites acknowledge their faults; they were humbly to seek forgiveness, which could not be done except they condemned themselves before God and so anticipated his judgment. On the mention of the fathers he denies that the faithful are looking for associates to extenuate their guilt; it aggravates their sin instead, since they confess not only their own guilt but what was as it were hereditary, brought with them from the womb. Ellicott makes the same point from the grammar, that inserting the conjunction weakens the force of the original: the wickedness Israel confesses is the iniquity of its fathers, inherited, accepted, and on the way to be perpetuated. Gill takes the confession as spoken for the few faithful among the people, sensible of their own sins and their ancestors’, having imitated and continued in the same. Clarke adds the melancholy note that the prophet did this on the people’s behalf, but they did not join him.
21:
The closing petitions come in short broken clauses, and Charles Ellicott hears the manner as part of the meaning: even in English, and more in the Hebrew, we seem to hear the broken accents and sobs of the agony of the prayer. The prophet can make no plea of extenuation, but he can appeal to the character of God, and urge with a bold anthropomorphism that mercy is truer to it than rigorous justice, and that the covenant with Israel pledges him to that mercy. John Gill makes the same distinction between what they deserve and what they ask: they had done what might justly render them abominable, and deprecate it not for their own sake but for the sake of God’s honour and glory. John Calvin explains whom the prayer speaks for: all boasted that they were children of God and gloried in the covenant made with Abraham, while hardly one in a thousand called on him from the heart; the prophet represents the true church, then very small.

The verbs are again disputed. Calvin surveys four renderings of the first pair and pronounces none correct, holding that the two verbs correspond to the pair used earlier—the first signifying rejection as worthless, the second as vile—so that the lines run scorn not, for thy name’s sake, abominate not the throne of thy glory. He quotes a translator who renders the pair spurn us not, dishonour not the throne of thy glory. On the throne, Clarke and Ellicott agree the temple is meant, Ellicott asking whether that place shall become a byword of reproach, scorned as a fool is scorned. John Wesley allows two references, the throne of the house of David, called the Lord’s throne, or the temple and the ark as the more special symbol of God’s presence. Adam Clarke raises the hardest objection. They had already broken the covenant and yet wish God to fulfil his part; they ceased to be his people by abandoning themselves to idolatry, and still wished him to defend them—but when the conditions of a covenant are broken by one party the other is not bound, and the covenant is annulled.

The last verse returns to the drought the chapter began with. Ellicott notes that the question is asked with reference to the drought which called forth the whole utterance, and that Israel remembers at last that God alone gives the rain and the fruitful seasons, turning to him in patient waiting; he finds an implied appeal to the history of Elijah. Gill adds that though one of the heathen gods bore the title of the god of rain, he could give no single drop, as another could not in the drought under Ahab. Clarke observes that it is the prerogative of the true God to send showers at the prayers of his people, and reads the closing clause as the last extremity: if thou do not undertake for us, we must be utterly ruined. Wesley states the argument formally, that the prophet reasons from the impossibility of help from any other quarter, the idols being nothing in themselves, and notes that Scripture constantly gives God the honour of giving rain. Calvin makes the argument itself the subject. The prophet avows despair in order to turn God to mercy—not that God needs reminding, but that he allows a familiar dealing with himself. If we reason stoically, even our prayers are superfluous, since God sees what we want and is ready enough to help; but such reasoning is wholly contrary to the genuine feeling of piety. As we flee to God when necessity urges, so we remind him, like a son unburdening his feelings in his father’s bosom; the faithful expostulate with him and bring forward everything by which he may be pacified, dealing with him after the manner of men about what was decreed before the creation of the world.
